name: YAFU (AVX-ECM backend)
workload: ECM curves per second (stage 1 and stage 2 both vectorised) on AVX-512 CPUs for inputs up to about a thousand bits, measured for the standalone AVX-ECM program that YAFU embeds as its default ECM backend on AVX-512 CPUs, versus GMP-ECM.
claimed_speedup: AVX-ECM 'has been observed to have about 1.5 to 2.5 times the throughput (curves/sec) of GMP-ECM, for numbers up to a thousand bits or so'; larger numbers are more efficient with GMP-ECM because AVX-ECM has no sub-quadratic multiplier (bbuhrow/avx-ecm README). The YAFU README itself carries no comparison numbers.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the 1.5-2.5x claim. avx-ecm README builds with 'make COMPILER=gcc730 SKYLAKEX=1' (gcc 7.3.0 or icc tested). The YAFU wiki SIQS tables list GCC 11.4 to 16.1 and Clang 17.0.6 (AOCC) with ISA labels (AVX512IFMA, AVX512BW, AVX2 BMI2, SSE41) but no flag strings.
stars_or_usage: 381 stars, 54 forks; README says YAFU has been referenced several times in the academic literature
tradeoffs: All-in-one automated factoring tool (trial division, Pollard rho, P-1, P+1, ECM, SIQS, SNFS/GNFS pipeline, expression language) rather than a library. Needs GMP; GMP-ECM optional; NFS needs the GGNFS lattice sievers (Linux and MinGW binaries bundled under factor/lasieve5_64/bin). msieve, ytools and ysieve are bundled in-tree since YAFU 3.0. AVX-ECM needs AVX-512 and runs constant-time curves in 208-bit steps with 8 curves per thread (32-bit digit option: 128-bit steps, 16 curves), with no sub-quadratic multiplication, so large inputs favour GMP-ECM. ISA-specific Windows builds: generic, sse41, avx2, avx512, avx512ifma.
caveats: Weak evidence for the listed baselines. (1) The YAFU repo README has no baseline comparison; the only GMP-ECM ratio is a first-party 'has been observed' sentence in the separate avx-ecm repo (BSD-2-Clause, 8 stars) with no CPU, compiler, flags, B1/B2 bounds, GMP-ECM version or benchmark code, so tier C. (2) The YAFU wiki Benchmarks page (https://github.com/bbuhrow/yafu/wiki/Benchmarks) lists SIQS wall-clock tables per CPU, compiler, ISA and thread count (for example 100-digit input on AMD EPYC 9174F, Clang 17.0.6 AOCC, AVX512IFMA, 32 threads, YAFU 3.1.9: 81.40 s sieve, 101.71 s total) but has no msieve, GMP-ECM or CADO-NFS column, so it is not a comparison against the named baselines. (3) WebSearch snippets of mersenneforum threads (pages blocked, not opened; snippet only) say YAFU SIQS was faster than msieve QS on old versions (a yafu-1.0 vs msieve-1.38 table with 0.97x-1.55x for 50-85 digits; another table at 85 digits with 386 s versus 873 s); those are 2008-2010 era numbers and are not recorded as evidence. (4) No NFS comparison against CADO-NFS was found. (5) Licence: no LICENSE file in the repo; the public-domain dedication is a source header (top/driver.c: placed in the public domain by its author), no patent grant; bundled components (msieve, cub, zlib, GGNFS siever binaries, CUDA ptx) keep their own terms and GMP/GMP-ECM linking brings LGPL/GPL obligations, hence 'mixed'.

name: mps-flash-attention (MPS Flash Attention)
language: Python, Swift, C++ (Metal kernels via metal-flash-attention)
workload: Forward attention, float16 by default, B=1, H=8, D=64 in the repo harness, sequence lengths 512 to 8192 and beyond, milliseconds per call of flash_attention versus F.scaled_dot_product_attention on Apple Silicon.
claimed_speedup: README table: sequence 1024 is 1.1-2.0x faster than PyTorch SDPA (crossover point); 2048 is 1.7-3.7x; 4096 is 2.0-3.9x; 8192+ is 3-4x (SDPA often OOMs). 'Average speedup: 1.8x across all configurations.' Also O(N) memory so 100K+ sequence lengths fit in unified memory.
hardware: 'Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4/M5)' only; no specific chip, core count or memory per table row
tradeoffs: Apple Silicon and macOS 14+ only; PyTorch 2.5 to 2.13 and Python 3.10-3.14 (wheel carries three C++ extension builds for torch ABI changes). Python API over a C++ extension, dlopen of a Swift bridge, and the metal-flash-attention kernel generator (git submodule pointing at the imperatormk fork of Philip Turner's project). Supports forward and backward, causal, boolean masks, sliding window, GQA/MQA, FP8/INT8/NF4 quantised KV cache, chunked 100K+ sequences, torch.compile custom op; dropout not supported.
caveats: The README gives speedup ranges per sequence length with no per-chip, per-dtype, per-head-dim or per-torch-version numbers, so the claim is first-party tier C even though the harness is public (test_benchmark.py: B=1, H=8, D=64, float16, 3 warmup and 10 timed runs with torch.mps.synchronize each iteration; mps_flash_attn/benchmark.py suite: 5 warmup and 20 runs, dtypes fp16/bf16, batch 1 and 4, head dim 64 and 128, causal and window variants). The baseline is PyTorch's own MPS SDPA path, which materialises the attention matrix (hence the OOMs at 8192+), so the win is against a non-flash baseline; the closest comparable, metal-flash-attention, is the engine underneath (kernel speed is largely inherited from it) and is not compared. The README clone URL and the PyPI project URLs point to mpsops/mps-flash-attention, which shows the same 14 stars and 3 forks and no 'forked from' header (apparently the same repository renamed or moved; not confirmed). TODO.md still lists 'Performance benchmarks vs naive MPS attention' as an open checkbox (stale planning file). Licence of the submodule fork was not checked.

name: zurand
baseline: dqrng (R package) and base R runif()/rnorm() (Mersenne Twister); randompack x256++simd (SIMD xoshiro256++) is the closest competitor
workload: R-level fills of n = 1e7 doubles (uniform and standard normal), millions of values per second, median of five rounds, every package in the same bench::mark() call, 1 thread and all threads, on a GitHub-hosted Linux x86_64 runner and an Apple M1 laptop.
claimed_speedup: Uniform, 1 thread, Linux x86_64 (AMD EPYC 7763): zurand xoshiro256pp 864 M/s versus randompack x256++simd 688, dqrng 368, base R runif() 104 (README: 1.26x over randompack; derived from page data: about 2.3x over dqrng and 8.3x over runif()). Apple M1, 1 thread: 2196 versus randompack 1918, dqrng 311, runif() 213. Gaussian, 1 thread: EPYC 366 versus randompack 355, dqrng 143, RcppZiggurat 125, rnorm() 28; M1 739 versus 718, 235, 225, 43. Threaded: EPYC 4 threads 1801 uniform versus randompack 684; M1 8 threads 4984 uniform and 3143 normal versus randompack 1888 and 708. README: single-thread lead over dqrng and RcppZiggurat is 2.3-7x.
compiler_and_flags: R CMD INSTALL build at -O2 ('an -O2 build, never devtools::load_all()', vignettes/performance.Rmd); compiler name and version not stated; OpenMP on Linux, R's own libomp on macOS; AVX2 and NEON paths; no fused multiply-add in normal sampling.
hardware: Linux: AMD EPYC 7763, 4 cores, AVX2, OpenMP, GitHub-hosted runner (2026-09-26). Apple M1 MacBook Air (4 performance plus 4 efficiency cores, 16 GB, NEON, mains power), 2026-09-27. README example output from an Intel Core i5-8500B (macOS, R 4.5.2, one thread).
stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks; version 0.1.0, not yet on CRAN ('from CRAN, once released')
tradeoffs: Stateless, key-based API: every value is a pure function of an immutable key and its position, never touches .Random.seed, output bit-identical across platforms and thread counts (including with OpenMP). Default engine xoshiro256++ reseeded every 512 values from Philox4x64-10 (Random123), PractRand clean to 1 TB; Philox4x64 and Threefry4x64 counter-based engines also available. Samplers: uniform, ziggurat normal (NumPy tables, plus McFarland method), integer, raw bits; ALTREP lazy vectors (full scans 1.6-2.7x slower than a materialised vector); C API header for LinkingTo packages. Changing engine changes every value. R package with C core, not a standalone C++ library.
caveats: None of the listed baselines (std::mt19937, xoshiro, PCG) is measured directly: competitors are R packages (dqrng, randompack, RcppZiggurat, sitmo) and base R, so numbers include R vector allocation and page faults (README/vignette: allocating and zeroing a 1e7 vector alone runs at about 1,250 M/s on the Linux runner; forcing 4 KiB pages cut the uniform fill from 837 to 242 M/s). Base R's runif()/rnorm() default is a Mersenne Twister with inversion, so the large gaps against it (derived from page data: about 8.3x uniform and 13x normal on EPYC, 1 thread) are largely algorithm and implementation choice. The real peer is randompack's SIMD xoshiro256++, where the single-thread lead is 1.26x (uniform, x86_64), 1.15x (M1), and only 1.01-1.08x for normals. The threaded rows are not like-for-like (the competitors have no threaded R-level entry point). Linux numbers come from a shared CI runner; the author notes the M1 CI runner moved by a third between runs and that zurand is tuned on Apple Silicon. Compiler not named, so tier C rather than A despite public workflow code (.github/workflows/benchmark.yml, tools/benchmark.R) and stated CPU models. Brand-new repository (commit history visible from 2026-09-27); first-party numbers only.

name: SpLLT (task-based sparse Cholesky)
workload: Parallel supernodal sparse Cholesky factorization of symmetric positive definite matrices on multicore, with OpenMP, StarPU and PaRSEC task backends, compared by the authors' papers with HSL_MA87; no numbers on any opened page.
claimed_speedup: None on opened pages (README and Sphinx docs have no performance data). WebSearch snippets of the authors' papers (pages blocked, not opened; snippet only) say the OpenMP and StarPU implementations show 'comparable performance' to HSL_MA87 on a multicore architecture, which is parity rather than a speedup.
stars_or_usage: 6 stars, 1 fork; NLAFET project code from STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory (BSD-3-Clause, copyright 2018 STFC)
tradeoffs: Fortran (with a C interface in interfaces/C and a C example) plus C++ kernel benchmarks (bench_kernels: gemm, potrf, syrk, trsm). Symmetric positive definite systems only. Needs SPRAL for the analysis phase, Metis 5.1, BLAS/LAPACK (MKL in the README examples), hwloc, CMake, and one runtime: StarPU, PaRSEC or OpenMP 4.0+. Sequential build by default.
caveats: No numeric comparison on any page opened, so tier D; claims of speed come only from search snippets saying 'comparable' to HSL_MA87, i.e. not faster. HSL_MA87 is itself a licensed HSL code. Comparisons against CHOLMOD or PaStiX were not found. Papers on epubs.stfc.ac.uk and aimsciences.org were EGRESS_BLOCKED. Last commit 2019-08-23 (abandoned), Travis CI badge only. Fortran rather than C++; callable from C++ through its C interface. Kept as a seed record for the catalogue; a paper-access retier could add the tables.

name: avxbls-sig (AVX-512 BLS signatures on BLS12-381)
baseline: blst (supranational/blst x64 assembly: blst_sign_pk_in_g1/g2, hash_to_g1/g2, pairing aggregation)
workload: Per-operation cycle counts (rdtsc average over many iterations) in test.c, AVX-512 vector routines versus blst scalar calls for scalar multiplication, point add/double, sk_to_pk, subgroup checks, hash-to-curve, signing in G1 and G2, and pairing-based aggregate/verify; the BLS scheme operations keygen, signing, aggregation, verification.
claimed_speedup: No numbers in the repo or README (test.c prints 'baseline avg cycles' versus 'vec avg cycles' at run time). From a WebSearch snippet only (page not opened): the associated paper 'Efficient SIMD Implementation of the BLS Signature Scheme Using Intel AVX-512' (TCHES 2026, IACR ePrint 2026/947) reports the vectorised BLS software is at least 1.57 times faster than the blst x64 assembly implementation on an Intel Core i3-1005G1 (Ice Lake).
compiler_and_flags: makefile: /opt/gcc-13.3/bin/gcc -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -m64 -mbmi2 -fwrapv -mtune=native -march=native -z noexecstack -w, linked against libblst.a built by build.sh (blst flags -O3 -fno-builtin -fPIC, -D__ADX__ when the CPU has ADX, -mno-avx).
hardware: Not stated in the repo; the paper snippet names an Intel Core i3-1005G1 (Ice Lake, AVX-512 IFMA).
stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks; sibling of the catalogued hchengv/avxbls (optimal ate pairing)
tradeoffs: Latency-optimised AVX-512 (IFMA-style 52-bit limb) code for x86-64 only, Linux oriented; built on blst (bundled in src_blst and a committed libblst.a) and links it for scalar fallbacks. Makefile hard-codes /opt/gcc-13.3/bin/gcc and -march=native. Covers keygen, signing, aggregation and verification on BLS12-381 (G1 and G2 variants). Research code with a cycle-count harness, no stable API documented.
caveats: Tier C: first-party repository, no published numbers in README or code, benchmark hardware absent from the repo; the 1.57x lower bound is from a search snippet of the paper (the ePrint 2026/947 page was EGRESS_BLOCKED and the TCHES page was not tried), so it is 'snippet only'. The paper is peer-reviewed per the snippet and its first author is named as Ganqin Liu, matching the repo owner, but the repo README has no paper link, so the link is inferred. Retier toward B (or A, since test.c and the compiler flags are public) once the paper's tables and CPU model can be read. rdtsc counts reference cycles, not core cycles, and the baseline is the single-signature blst API, not blst's multi-threaded or batch paths. No aggregate throughput or batching comparison. A prebuilt libblst.a binary is committed.
